summary:
Satellites have tracked fire hotspots for over 20 years, but the record is split between MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). The two count the same fires differently, so the raw record shows a false jump in fire activity when VIIRS arrives, and fire managers can’t tell what is normal for their area.

We built Emberline, a web app that merges NASA FIRMS hotspots from both sensors into one consistent record from 2001 to today. To stop overlapping detections from inflating counts, we count each fire once as “burning cells”: roughly 2 km grid squares with active fire on a given day. We then learn, month by month, how the sensors differ during the years both flew, and use that to bridge the MODIS-only years. Estimated values are labelled and carry uncertainty bands.

Users select any area and get a burning activity calendar, a now-vs-normal comparison, critical fire periods, fire rankings and downloadable CSV files. We tested it on the 2022 Corrientes, Argentina wildfires. Our alert, fixed using only past data, fired N days before/after the first emergency decree.
details:
Emberline has two parts.

1. A harmonization pipeline

  • It downloads MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) hotspots from NASA FIRMS and normalizes them into one schema, using the local solar day.
  • It resolves overlapping detections at four levels: duplicate records, multiple pixels of one fire, the same fire seen by several satellites on one day, and multi-day fires grouped into fire events.
  • From the overlap years (2012 onward), it computes monthly bridge factors that bring MODIS-only periods onto the same scale as the combined record. Uncertainty bands come from resampling the overlap years.
  • It uses one VIIRS satellite per day, so newly launched satellites don’t create artificial jumps. This matters now: Suomi NPP has stopped delivering data, and NOAA-20 takes over automatically.
  • Days with no satellite coverage are shown as “no data”, never as zero.

2. A web application.

  • Users draw an area, enter latitude/longitude, or choose a preset.
    • the Ember Calendar (year × month activity, 2001–present, colour-blind-safe colours)
    • a Fire Clock of the seasonal pattern
    • current month vs historical median, compared over the same days so it’s fair
    • a Normal / Elevated / Extreme status
    • the area’s critical fire window
    • how the current fire ranks against past ones
  • Exports: hotspot CSV, summary CSV, chart images, and a one-page field card.

Benefits

  • The record is consistent whichever sensor saw a fire, so fire managers can compare any month with 20+ years of history.
    • Response Station for emergency responders and firefighters (“Is it bad right now?”)
    • Ranger Post for land managers (“When does this area usually burn?”)
    • Research Lab for scientists (method, validation, raw exports)
  • It keeps the 25-year history usable as MODIS retires.

Validation

  • Hold-out test: we hid VIIRS one year at a time and predicted it from MODIS. Result: [x]% monthly error, [x]% bias, [x]% of values inside the 90% band.
  • Seam Splitter: drag a slider to see the false 2012 jump disappear in the harmonized line.
  • “Would we have seen it coming?” replay: we replayed Corrientes, Dec 2021 – Feb 2022, day by day. The alert rule was fixed on 2003–2021 data before testing. We report its timing against the official decrees, and how often it fired in other seasons ([X] of 19), so judges can see its false-alarm rate.

Intended impact

The goal is to give fire services an early, sensor-independent signal that “this isn’t normal for this place and time of year”. It also helps land managers plan around critical periods, and gives researchers a consistent long-term fire record. The pipeline doesn’t depend on the region, so it can scale to any country, since FIRMS data is global.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript
  • Pipeline: pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, Parquet, Shapely
  • Backend: FastAPI, hosted on Hugging Face Spaces
  • Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL (OpenStreetMap/CARTO basemaps)
  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS 375 m); geoBoundaries for administrative boundaries
  • Deployment: Vercel (frontend) Railway (backend)
  • AI: AI assistance was used for code generation and planning, as disclosed in the AI section. All results in the app are deterministic and traceable to NASA data.

Creativity

  • We count fires, not hotspots, so overlap is solved by design rather than patched afterwards.
  • The bridge works in both directions, covering the MODIS-only past and the VIIRS-only future.
  • Early warning is tested honestly against a real disaster, not just claimed.

Factors we considered

  • Different sensor resolutions, sensitivities and overpass times
  • Satellite launches and retirements
  • Missing data vs no fire
  • Fair month-to-date comparisons
  • Uncertainty in estimated years
  • Avoiding hindsight bias in the alert rule
  • Colour-blind accessibility and reduced motion
  • Low bandwidth, with cached fallbacks so the demo never fails
  • Free and open data and tools
  • The different needs of responders, land managers and scientist
